Here is the verse-by-verse commentary on Jeremiah 9, compiled from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Jeremiah 9: Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — "Oh, that my head were a spring of water…"

**Traditional Reading:** In the Hebrew Bible this verse properly concludes chapter 8. Jeremiah, having just lamented the coming fall of Judah (Jer 8:18–22), now poetically expresses that he does not have enough tears to adequately grieve over "the slain of the daughter of my people." The Pulpit Commentary notes that this "sudden conversion of a strong-felt metaphor into something to be actually realized in nature, is strictly and strikingly natural" — the prophet wishes his grief could take physical form as an inexhaustible fountain. David Guzik (Enduring Word) adds that Jeremiah's tears were good because they were tender and sympathetic; quoting John Trapp: "Such waters will be turned into wine, at the wedding-day of the Lamb; for which purpose also they are kept safe in God's bottle (Psalm 56:8)." Ellicott notes the Hebrew form "Who will give my head waters?" is the natural idiom for desire, as in Latin.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-9/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html

---

### v. 2 — "If only I had a traveler's lodge in the wilderness…"

**Traditional Reading:** The prophet wishes for a "khan" or "caravanserai" — a remote desert shelter for travelers — so he could escape his corrupt people. His grief over coming judgment is mixed with disgust over their sin. Ellicott explains that a "lodging place of wayfaring men" was like the "inn" of Genesis 42:27 or the "habitation of Chimham" near Bethlehem (2 Sam 19:40). The Pulpit Commentary notes Cowper's famous echo: "Oh for a lodge in some vast wilderness!" Guzik cites Feinberg: "Even a lonely lodging in the desert was preferable to the soul anguish he experienced in the midst of his people." The people are called "adulterers" — both spiritually (idolatry) and literally (Jer 5:8). The word translated "crowd" (or "assembly") is the Hebrew term used for solemn assemblies at pilgrimage feasts — a bitter irony.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-9/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html

---

### v. 3 — "They bend their tongues like bows; lies prevail over truth…"

**Traditional Reading:** The metaphor pictures the tongue as a bow that shoots arrows of lies. The JFB Commentary renders it: "they direct lies on their tongue as their bow" (cf. Ps 64:3–4). Ellicott notes that the older rendering "they are not valiant for the truth upon the earth" — though beloved as a proverbial phrase — more accurately means "they are not mighty for truth (faithfulness) in the land," i.e., they do not rule faithfully. The root problem is stated at the end: "they do not take Me into account" — they do not "know" the LORD in the sense of acknowledging and obeying Him (1 Sam 2:12; Job 18:21). Guzik, citing Thompson, notes: "The verb yada, 'know,' denotes much more than intellectual knowledge but rather that deep intimate knowledge that follows the personal commitment of one life to another."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-9/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/9.htm (excerpts from search)

### v. 4 — "Let everyone guard against his neighbor; do not trust any brother…"

**Traditional Reading:** The corruption is so pervasive that the elementary bonds of society are dissolved. "Every brother will utterly supplant" uses the Hebrew verb that gave Jacob his name — "the supplanter" (Gen 25:26, 27:36). Ellicott observes: "Jeremiah seems to say that the people have forfeited their claims to the name of the true Israel. Every brother Israelite is found to be a thorough-paced Jacob." The Pulpit Commentary adds that this depicts a society where suspicion becomes the natural attitude even of a good man — the result of clinging to an unspiritual, merely ritualistic religion. JFB notes "supplant" literally means "trip up by the heel" (cf. Hos 12:3). "Every friend spreads slander" — literally "goeth about as a slanderer."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/9.htm (excerpts)

### v. 5 — "Each one betrays his friend; no one tells the truth…"

**Traditional Reading:** The people have "taught their tongues to speak lies" — an intimation of the unnaturalness of vice; lying had to be learned and practiced. Adam Clarke (cited by Guzik) exclaims: "O, what a drudgery is sin! And how much labour must a man take in order to get to hell!" JFB notes: "weary themselves — are at laborious pains to act perversely. Sin is a hard bondage (Hab 2:13)." Ellicott: the word "deceive" here carries the sense of mockery that both deludes and derides.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-9/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html

---

### v. 6 — "You dwell in the midst of deception; in their deceit they refuse to know Me…"

**Traditional Reading:** The address is disputed. Jerome thought it addressed to the prophet personally, but the Targum and most modern commentators (including the Pulpit Commentary) see it as addressed to the Jewish people collectively: "Thou dwellest surrounded by deceit on every side." The greatest cost of embracing deception is that it creates a fundamental distance from God, who is a God of truth. Guzik notes: "Through deceit they refuse to know Me — this is the greatest cost. Since God is a God of truth, those who love the lie have a fundamental distance from Him."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-9/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm

---

### v. 7 — "Behold, I will refine them and test them…"

**Traditional Reading:** God falls back on the imagery of the metal refiner (already used in Jer 6:28–30; cf. Isa 48:10; Mal 3:3). The purpose is not destruction but purification. The Pulpit Commentary: "Purification, not destruction, is the object of the judgment which is threatened! Strange that mercy should find place, after the offence of the criminal has been found so grievous!" Ellicott: "The evil has come to such a pass that nothing is left but the melting of the fiery furnace of affliction. How else could He act for the daughter of His people? The balm of Gilead had proved ineffectual. The disease required a severer remedy." Charles Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) preached: "The Lord is so resolved to save his people, that he will use the sternest possible means rather than lose any of those whom he loves."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-9/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html

### v. 8 — "Their tongues are deadly arrows; they speak deception…"

**Traditional Reading:** This echoes Psalm 55:21. The Hebrew text (consonants), followed by the Septuagint and Vulgate, reads "a murderous arrow" rather than "a sharpened arrow." The Pulpit Commentary notes this distinction. The description of speaking peace "with his mouth" while setting a trap "in his heart" (lit. "inwardly") paints a picture of calculated treachery.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html

---

### v. 9 — "Should I not punish them for these things? … Should I not avenge Myself on such a nation as this?"

**Traditional Reading:** This is a repeated warning, already given in Jeremiah 5:9 and 5:29. Ellicott notes the "emphasis of iteration." Guzik points out that the term goy ("nation") is used for Israel here — a term regularly used of non-Israelite peoples, suggesting "Jeremiah had come to regard the people as no different in their behavior from the goyim, the peoples outside the covenant."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-9/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html

---

### v. 10 — "I will take up a weeping and wailing for the mountains…"

**Traditional Reading:** Jeremiah breaks in upon God's threats of wrath with his own lament. The Hebrew preposition can mean both "upon" and "on account of" — the prophet sees himself upon the mountains, lamenting because they are "burned up." The Pulpit Commentary notes that the "habitations" should rather be "pastures": the country once covered with grazing flocks is now so utterly waste that even birds cannot find subsistence. JFB: "Jeremiah breaks in upon Jehovah's threats of wrath with lamentation for his desolated country."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/9.htm (excerpts)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html

---

### v. 11 — "I will make Jerusalem a heap of rubble, a haunt for jackals…"

**Traditional Reading:** The Hebrew word translated "dragons" in the KJV means "jackals" — literally "a howler." Ellicott notes the error probably arose from the word's resemblance to terms for "serpent" or "whale." The image is of total desolation: once-bustling cities become uninhabited ruins where only wild animals dwell. The Pulpit Commentary observes that the utterances of the prophets stand seamlessly alongside those of Jehovah — "a true prophet has no personal views."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html

---

### vv. 12–14 — "Who is the man wise enough to understand this? … Because they have forsaken My law…"

**Traditional Reading:** The prophet poses a rhetorical question: who among the "wise men" (scribes, religious teachers) can explain why the land is destroyed? The answer is not given by the sages — they are "ashamed" (Jer 8:9) — so Yahweh Himself answers: "Because they have forsaken My law." The Pulpit Commentary explains that "My law which I set before them" refers not only to the Sinai legislation but to the oral exhibition of the Torah by the prophets. The people walked "after the stubbornness of their own hearts" (the Hebrew means "stubbornness," not merely "imagination" as in some older translations) and "after the Baals." Guzik notes: God designed us to be worshipful, obedient beings; when we reject His word, we redirect worship toward self and cultural gods. Harrison adds that Baal worship "had proved attractive to many generations of Israelites" through its lewd, orgiastic cult.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-9/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html

### vv. 15–16 — "I will feed this people wormwood and give them poisoned water… I will scatter them among the nations…"

**Traditional Reading:** "Wormwood" (a bitter plant, probably Artemisia) and "water of gall" (the poppy, per Tristram) symbolize the bitter privations of captivity (cf. Lam 3:15; Deut 29:17–18). The scattering "among the nations" fulfills covenant curses (Deut 28:64; Lev 26:33). The Pulpit Commentary notes that even in exile they would have no rest — "I will send a sword after them" — yet the nation as such was, through its Divine calling, indestructible; it is the unbelievers who are referred to. JFB observes: because their fathers taught them Baal worship (v. 14), the children shall be scattered to lands their fathers never knew.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/jeremiah/9.htm (excerpts)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html

### vv. 17–18 — "Summon the wailing women; send for the most skillful among them…"

**Traditional Reading:** In the ancient Near East, professional mourning women were hired for funerals. They used plaintive cries, bared their breasts, flailed their arms, threw dust on their heads, and disheveled their hair (cf. 2 Chr 35:25; Eccl 12:5; Amos 5:16; Matt 9:23). Guzik cites Feinberg's description of these "skillful wailing women." The Pulpit Commentary, quoting the 18th-century traveler Dr. Shaw, notes: "They perform their parts with such proper sounds, gestures, and commotions, that they rarely fail to work up the assembly into some extraordinary pitch of thoughtfulness and sorrow." The purpose ("that our eyes may overflow with tears") was to provide a vent for sorrow — the piercing notes of hired mourners were meant to help the truly afflicted release their grief.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-9/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm

---

### vv. 19–20 — "The sound of wailing is heard from Zion… Teach your daughters to wail…"

**Traditional Reading:** The lament from Zion reflects the shame of exile: "We have abandoned the land because our dwellings have been torn down." The Pulpit Commentary clarifies that "forsaken" means "left" (not voluntary abandonment) and "our dwellings have cast us out" means "they have cast down our dwellings." Verse 20 instructs women to teach their daughters the art of lamentation — the deaths would be so numerous that there would not be enough professional mourners. Ellicott draws a parallel to Jesus' words to the daughters of Jerusalem: "Weep for yourselves and for your children" (Luke 23:27–28).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html

---

### vv. 21–22 — "Death has climbed in through our windows… corpses… like dung upon the open field…"

**Traditional Reading:** "Death" here specifically means "pestilence" (as in Jer 15:2), the most dreaded foe of a besieged city. Ellicott: it "creeps in with its fatal taint at the windows, even though the invader is for a time kept at bay, and cuts off the children who else would play in the courtyard." The ideal picture from Zechariah 8:5 — children playing in the streets — is reversed. In v. 22, the dead bodies lie unburied "like dung upon the open field." Guzik (citing Feinberg) explains the harvest imagery: "The custom was for a reaper to hold in his arm what a few strokes of his sickle had cut. Then he put it down… So death was to cover the ground with corpses, but the carcasses would lie there unburied because of the paucity of survivors." To the ancient Hebrew, failure to bury the dead was a double disgrace. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the words "Speak, Thus saith the LORD" are absent from the Septuagint and are stylistically unusual for Jeremiah — they were probably not in the original Hebrew text.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-9/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html

### vv. 23–24 — "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom… but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me…"

This is one of the most-quoted passages in Jeremiah, used by Paul in 1 Corinthians 1:31 and 2 Corinthians 10:17.

**Traditional Reading:** The "wise man" (hakam) refers specifically to the scribe or recognized teacher of the people (Ellicott; cf. Jer 8:9). God does not rebuke the instinct to glory — He redirects it. Guzik: "The problem with man is not that he longs to glory in something; the problem is that he generally glories in the wrong things." Kidner (cited by Guzik): "There is a contrast between the three fading glories of Jeremiah 9:23 and the three unfading ones of Jeremiah 9:24: the faithful love, justice, and righteousness which are God's gifts to us before ever they are his expectations from us." The knowledge of God has specific doctrinal content — it is not a vague mystical experience but an encounter with His hesed (covenant love), His mishpat (judgment/justice), and His tsedaqah (righteousness).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-9/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html

**Reformed / Calvin:** John Calvin (Commentary on Jeremiah, accessible via CCEL) stressed that this passage was not "abrupt" but connected to the preceding judgment. The Jews were "swollen with false confidence" — proud of their wisdom, wealth, and power — and Jeremiah declares that "men foolishly gloried, while they set up their riches, or their strength, or their wisdom, in opposition to God; for all these things would vanish away like smoke." The Monergism article elaborates: "All earthly glorying is sin; glorying that is spiritual, that is based upon possessing a spiritual good, that is right glorying!" Knowledge of God here "cannot be a mere intellectual knowledge about God" but must be "a personal knowledge… that has seeped down into our heart so that a relationship results." Yet it also has "specific doctrinal content" — it is "not to be confused with emotional feelings which are merely subjective." The Monergism writer connects this knowledge directly to the cross: "God provides the sacrifice who satisfies for all our sins, and God justifies the ungodly… In this we are to glory, and in nothing else!"

- https://www.monergism.com/glorying-knowing-god
- https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_jeremiah_and_lamentations_volume_1/jeremiah_9_23-24.htm

**Pulpit Commentary (Anglican/evangelical):** The Pulpit Commentary offers a nuanced theological exposition of the three attributes. "Loving-kindness" (hesed) is "not to be understood in a vague and general sense of the love of God to all mankind; the term has a special connotation with regard to the Israelitish people. God shows loving-kindness to those with whom he is in covenant." "Judgment" (mishpat) means Jehovah as King helps the poor and weak to their right and punishes the wrongdoer. "Righteousness" (tsedaqah) is a wider term: "the quality which leads its subject to adhere to a fixed rule of conduct. God's rule is his covenant; hence 'righteousness' shows itself in all such acts as tend to the full realizing of the covenant with Israel, including the 'plan of salvation.'"

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm

### vv. 25–26 — "I will punish all who are circumcised yet uncircumcised… Egypt, Judah, Edom…"

**Traditional Reading:** The key phrase is difficult. The KJV "circumcised with the uncircumcised" is misleading. Ellicott translates: "all those that are circumcised in uncircumcision" — those who have the outward sign but not the inward purity it symbolizes. The Pulpit Commentary notes that circumcision was practiced by Egyptians (as evidenced by bas-reliefs at Karnak), Edomites, and ancient Arabs — so the physical rite was not unique to Israel. This makes Jeremiah's point sharper: Judah is "sandwiched in between Egypt and Edom" (Spurgeon, cited by Guzik). The reference to those who "clip the hair of their temples" (lit. "corner-clipped") describes certain Arab tribes who, according to Herodotus (3:8), shaved their temples in honor of Bacchus — a practice forbidden in Leviticus 19:27. Ellicott calls the epithet "one of scorn," like calling someone "round-head." The conclusion is devastating: "all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart." Jeremiah anticipates Paul in Romans 2:25–29 — the true circumcision is "in the spirit, not in the letter."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-9.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/9.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-9/

## Points of Denominational Emphasis

### Reformed / Calvinist
On vv. 23–24, the Reformed tradition emphasizes that "knowing God" is not merely intellectual but involves a heart-level, relational knowledge produced by grace — yet it has objective doctrinal content centered on God's sovereignty, covenant love (hesed), justice, and righteousness. Calvin taught that men "foolishly gloried" in their own resources against God, and that true glorying is found only in God's self-revelation. The Monergism article explicitly ties this knowledge to "the great works of God in the cross and resurrection of Jesus" and justification by faith: "God justifies the ungodly and quiets their fearful consciences by preaching to them their innocence by faith in the blood of Christ." On vv. 25–26, the distinction between outward circumcision and circumcision of the heart aligns with the Reformed covenant theology emphasis that the outward sign without inward spiritual reality profits nothing — a principle applied also to baptism in Reformed sacramentology.

- https://www.monergism.com/glorying-knowing-god
- https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_jeremiah_and_lamentations_volume_1/jeremiah_9_23-24.htm

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word – David Guzik)
Guzik's commentary (used widely in charismatic circles) emphasizes that the Hebrew word for "know" (yada) in vv. 3 and 24 "denotes much more than intellectual knowledge but rather that deep intimate knowledge that follows the personal commitment of one life to another." On vv. 23–24, he stresses that "God did not rebuke man's instinct to look for glory; instead, God guided that instinct to its proper destination." The knowledge of God is described as including an experiential "encounter with His lovingkindness, His judgment, and His righteousness." On v. 7 (refining), Spurgeon is quoted: "The Lord is so resolved to save his people, that he will use the sternest possible means rather than lose any of those whom he loves" — resonating with charismatic/Pentecostal views of God's purifying work through trials.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-9/
